name: Lemon Verbena
summary: A lemon-scented woody shrub grown for aromatic leaves. It can reach several feet outdoors, is frost-sensitive in cold climates, and may drop leaves when overwintered indoors; extension sources describe pruning, fresh/dried leaf harvest and occasional pests.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Aloysia citrodora and lists Aloysia triphylla and Lippia citriodora among its synonyms. NC State Extension uses the accepted name and describes lemon verbena as a fragrant culinary shrub; no cultivar is specified.

cultivation.short: Full sun outdoors; protect from frost in cold climates
cultivation.guidance: Illinois Extension recommends a container in frost-prone climates so the plant can move indoors before frost. It describes full sun outdoors, uniformly moist but well-drained media, and reduced fertilizer indoors. Illinois calls it a heavy feeder and suggests general-purpose liquid fertilizer about every two weeks in its outdoor/container context; this is not a universal schedule or a hydroponic nutrient recipe. Illinois also notes that overwintered indoor plants may lose leaves, which is a reported seasonal response in that context.

growth.short: Woody shrub; 6–8 ft in ground or 2–4 ft in a pot (NC State)
growth.guidance: NC State Extension describes a woody perennial shrub and reports about 6–8 ft tall and wide in the ground versus 2–4 ft tall and wide in a pot in its regional profile. The potted range is a gardening context, not a prediction for a compact indoor system. In its native habitat it may grow 10–15 ft; that native-range description is not a home-garden target.

maintenance.short: Prune or harvest periodically to maintain form
maintenance.guidance: Illinois Extension says occasional pruning or frequent harvest helps maintain plant form; NC State Extension notes early-spring pruning encourages bushier growth. Timing is guidance for their temperate-region contexts, not a universal calendar.

harvest.short: Harvest aromatic leaves for fresh or dried use
harvest.guidance: Illinois Extension describes harvesting leaves as needed through the season and using them fresh or dried. Leaves are used to flavor beverages and foods; no medicinal efficacy is claimed.

propagation.short: Stem cuttings are the recommended reliable route in North America
propagation.guidance: NC State Extension recommends stem cuttings because seed set is variable in North America. This is a propagation route, not a seed-germination protocol; no timing or rooting recipe is added beyond what the source supports.

flowering.short: Small white-to-pale-lilac flowers appear in midsummer to early fall
flowering.guidance: NC State Extension describes fragrant small white-to-pale-lilac flowers from midsummer into early fall.

problems.short: No serious problems reported; occasional sap-feeding pests occur
problems.guidance: NC State Extension reports no serious problems but lists aphids, whiteflies, mealybugs and spider mites as occasional pests. Treat these as possible warning signs, not inevitable infestations or a cultivar-specific susceptibility claim.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The selected extension sources describe soil and container growing, not hydroponic production.

growthHabits.reason: A woody shrub habit is documented, but that alone does not establish fit for a Garden X machine.

height.reason: Regional ground and pot dimensions vary and do not establish an indoor-system mature height.

spread.reason: No indoor mature spread is supported.

spacing.reason: No machine pod spacing is established.

light.reason: Outdoor full-sun guidance is not an indoor grow-light classification.

name: Cuban Oregano
summary: A fleshy-leaved aromatic herb in the mint family, distinct from true oregano (Origanum). NC State Extension says stem cuttings root easily and recommends protection from intense hot sun; no seed protocol is supplied.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Coleus amboinicus in Lamiaceae; Plectranthus amboinicus is a historically used alternative taxonomy/name. NC State Extension's page uses Plectranthus amboinicus and lists Cuban oregano among its common names. This plant is not Origanum vulgare.

cultivation.short: Use filtered or partial shade and a well-drained medium
cultivation.guidance: NC State Extension recommends protection from hot summer sun; UF/IFAS describes partial shade and well-drained soil. Both are outdoor garden contexts, not indoor grow-light tiers or hydroponic instructions. UF/IFAS says occasional irrigation may suffice in its Florida context; do not apply that as a fixed schedule to containers or systems.

growth.short: Fleshy aromatic foliage on a spreading perennial
growth.guidance: NC State Extension describes young succulent stems that become semi-woody and reports 1–3 feet of height and spread in its regional profile. UF/IFAS reports about 19 inches tall in its Florida garden context. These are source-contextual, non-cultivar dimensions rather than an indoor-system target.

care.short: Avoid persistent wetness; protect from frost
care.guidance: UF/IFAS describes only occasional irrigation in its Florida garden context and identifies the plant as frost-tender. Treat these as regional cues: use a draining medium, check actual container moisture, and protect the plant from freezing rather than following a fixed watering calendar.

harvest.short: Aromatic leaves are used sparingly for flavor
harvest.guidance: NC State Extension describes fragrant leaves used for seasoning; UF/IFAS says the crushed-leaf aroma is strongly camphor/menthol-like and that the herb can overpower other flavors. This is culinary context, not a medicinal claim or a prescribed harvest interval.

problems.short: Cold injury is a documented regional risk
problems.guidance: UF/IFAS identifies Cuban oregano as frost-tender and recommends movable pots for cooler climates. This supports protecting it from freezing; it does not establish an exact minimum temperature or promise indoor-system performance.

propagation.short: Stem cuttings are an easy documented propagation route
propagation.guidance: NC State Extension says Cuban oregano is very easy to propagate from stem cuttings and can also be divided in spring. This supports vegetative propagation, not a claim that seed propagation is biologically impossible.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The selected source describes garden cultivation and cuttings, not hydroponic production.

growthHabits.reason: Herbaceous perennial and semi-woody stems are documented, but controlled-system fit is not.

height.reason: The extension dimensions are regional landscape guidance, not an indoor-system mature height.

spread.reason: The extension dimensions do not establish a machine-compatible spread.

light.reason: Outdoor sun-protection advice is not an indoor grow-light classification.
